title: Abstract Pronominal Anaphora in Three Registers of English
research_question: How do the distribution, referential functions, pronoun choices, and non-nominal antecedent properties of abstract pronominal anaphora vary across newswire, spontaneous dialogue, and planned speech?
methodology: O'Donnell compiled a corpus spanning newswire text, spontaneous dialogue, and planned speech. All instances of the pronouns "it", "this", and "that" were annotated, together with their non-nominal antecedents when present. The study compared pronoun frequencies, referential functions, and grammatical characteristics of non-nominal antecedents across the three registers; only the abstract was accessible, so sample sizes, detailed coding procedures, and statistical analyses could not be inspected.

key_findings.finding: The frequencies of different referential functions vary across the three registers.
Pronoun choice and the referential function served by a pronoun vary by register.
The grammatical structures of non-nominal antecedents vary across the text types.
The difficulty of annotating the relevant anaphoric phenomena varies across the material studied.
The authors conclude that spoken discourse exhibits a range of pronominal reference and non-nominal antecedent patterns that may not be recoverable from even very large newswire collections.
The accessible abstract provides no empirical analysis of multi-question messages, unanswered subquestions, scoped approval or rejection, or proposition-level reply-to alignment.

limitations: Only the abstract could be read because the repository's full-text download returned HTTP 403, so detailed corpus size, annotation agreement, statistical tests, and numerical results could not be verified.
The study compares linguistic registers rather than workplace email or enterprise communication specifically.
Its central relation is pronominal anaphora between a pronoun and an antecedent, not the scope of a reply over one or more propositions in a prior message.

Although spontaneous dialogue is included, the accessible abstract does not indicate that multi-question turns, unanswered questions, approvals, rejections, or multi-antecedent response links were separately annotated.
The accessible source does not establish public availability of the compiled corpus or research code.
raw_claims: Abstract anaphora can refer to discourse entities such as events, facts, and propositions.
Abstract-anaphora antecedents can have non-nominal syntactic structure.
The corpus combines newswire, spontaneous dialogue, and planned speech.
The pronouns "it", "this", and "that" were annotated throughout the corpus.
Non-nominal antecedents associated with those pronouns were also annotated.
The study compares pronoun frequency, referential function, and antecedent characteristics across registers.
Multiple aspects of abstract-pronoun usage differ between the three registers.
The accessible abstract does not report an annotation of reply scope between questions and answers.
